html:
A castle on low ground by Tokyo Bay, first built in 1457 by the warrior and poet Ōta Dōkan in the village of Edo. It grew into the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns and the heart of modern Tokyo.

For more than a century it was a modest frontier fort. In 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi gave the Kantō region to Tokugawa Ieyasu, who made Edo his base. After he became shogun in 1603, the castle was rebuilt as the largest in Japan, with rings of moats, stone walls and a tall keep. Lords from across the country were made to pay for the work and to live part of each year in Edo, which made the town around it boom.

The great keep burned in a city fire in 1657 and was never rebuilt. In 1868 the last shogun handed the castle over without a fight, and the young Meiji Emperor moved in. Its inner grounds are now the Imperial Palace.
